content: {"id": "47c163f3-ea97-4310-b4a2-589c337e037d", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Hypothetical for the DynamoDB latency skill \u2014 no AWS calls. Table catalog-test, 3-hour window. Query shows SystemErrors of 240 across 12 consecutive periods 13:00\u201313:11, and FaultInjectionServiceInducedErrors for Query is exactly 240 in the same periods. Query p99 rose to 130 ms against its 7-day baseline of 30 ms in those periods, with thousands of requests per period; p50 stayed at baseline. Our SystemErrors alarm fired. Is DynamoDB having a service problem?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "61aa43a7-1b40-4e20-a70b-5c532d2dcb08", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "No — that pattern points to a deliberate fault injection test, not a genuine DynamoDB service problem.

Here's why:

- **SystemErrors exactly matches FaultInjectionServiceInducedErrors** — 240 vs 240, period by period, for the same 12 consecutive minutes. That one-to-one correspondence is the signature of FIS (Fault Injection Simulator) or a similar chaos-testing tool deliberately injecting errors into DynamoDB calls, not organic service-side faults.
- **p50 latency is unaffected** — if DynamoDB itself were struggling, you'd expect broad-based latency degradation across the distribution, not just the tail. A flat p50 with a p99 spike to 130 ms (from a 30 ms baseline) while thousands of requests per period succeed normally is consistent with a subset of requests being intentionally failed/delayed by an injected fault, while the rest sail through untouched.
- **The p99 rise is proportionate to the injected-error count**, not to overall traffic — real DynamoDB-side degradation tends to show up as broader throttling (ThrottledRequests), elevated error rates across request types, or correlated regional/service health signals, none of which you're describing here.

The alarm firing is working as designed — SystemErrors spiked, so it fired. But the root cause is the fault injection experiment, not an underlying DynamoDB outage or degradation. I'd check whether there's a known/scheduled FIS experiment or chaos-engineering run targeting the `catalog-test` table around 13:00–13:11 to confirm — that would close the loop.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
